newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: COMPETITION PROMPTS SAFRICA'S BOKOMO/SASKO MERGER.
newsitem.headline: COMPETITION PROMPTS SAFRICA'S BOKOMO/SASKO MERGER.

text.p: Increased foreign competition brought on by the opening up of the South African market was one of the main reasons behind the merger of non-listed companies Bokomo and Sasko, Bokomo chief executive Andre Hanekom said on Friday.
"The big thing that forced us together was South Africa opening up to world markets and competition coming in from outside," he told Reuters after the proposed merger had been announced.
"We felt that both of us were maybe significant players in South Africa when we were protected, but we did not have the critical mass to survive the longer term."

The two former co-operatives announced on Friday that their boards had agreed to merge the two limited companies to form a new food giant with combined assets of 1.5 billion rand, annual turnover of more than 3.5 billion and projected annual earnings of about 130 million rand.
The merger still has to be approved by shareholders and will be discussed with the Competition Board.
Hanekom and Sasko chief executive Stephan Bellingan told reporters they hoped to get shareholders' approval by the end of June and that the new company would be in place by October 1.
Because the two companies' activities only overlapped in milling and baking in the Western and some parts of the Eastern Cape, they believed that the Competition Board would approve the merger.
"We have not decided on a name yet," Bellingan said.
Asked if a listing on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange was likely, Hanekom said that this had not been the reason for the merger but added "it may happen if we have a good reason."
If it did list, it would rank between fourth and seventh in the food sector and be well placed in the top 100 companies, Bellingan said.
The two companies export food products worth about 70 to 80 million rand and are considering setting up baking and other food-related production activities in neighbouring countries.

They have a market share of between 25 to 35 percent in milling and baking sectors, breakfast foods and frozen foods. They also have smaller niche markets of between two to seven percent in products such as pasta and broilers.
